arXiv:2203.09436v4 [math.OC] 08 Jan 2023

Stochastic Halpern Iteration with Variance Reduction
for Stochastic Monotone Inclusions

Xufeng Cai Note: Department of Computer Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Madison. XC (xcai74@wisc.edu), CS (chaobing.song@wisc.edu), JD (jelena@cs.wisc.edu).    Chaobing Song††footnotemark:    Cristóbal Guzmán Note: Institute for Mathematical and Computational Eng., Facultad de Matemáticas and Escuela de Ingeniería, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. crguzmanp@mat.uc.cl.    Jelena Diakonikolas††footnotemark:
Abstract

We study stochastic monotone inclusion problems, which widely appear in machine learning applications, including robust regression and adversarial learning. We propose novel variants of stochastic Halpern iteration with recursive variance reduction. In the cocoercive—and more generally Lipschitz-monotone—setup, our algorithm attains ϵ\epsilon norm of the operator with 𝒪⁡(1ϵ3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{3}}) stochastic operator evaluations, which significantly improves over state of the art 𝒪⁡(1ϵ4)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}}) stochastic operator evaluations required for existing monotone inclusion solvers applied to the same problem classes. We further show how to couple one of the proposed variants of stochastic Halpern iteration with a scheduled restart scheme to solve stochastic monotone inclusion problems with 𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/ϵ)ϵ2){\mathcal{O}}(\frac{\log(1/\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}}) stochastic operator evaluations under additional sharpness or strong monotonicity assumptions.

1 Introduction

Recent trends in machine learning (ML) involve the study of models whose solutions do not reduce to optimization but rather to equilibrium conditions. Standard examples include generative adversarial networks, adversarially robust training of ML models, and training of ML models under notions of fairness. It turns out that several of these equilibrium conditions (including, but not limited to, first-order stationary points, saddle-points, and Nash equilibria of minimax games) can be cast as solutions to a monotone inclusion problem, which is defined as the problem of computing a zero of a (maximal) monotone operator F:ℝd→ℝdF:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} (see (MI) for a formal definition). In the context of min-max optimization problems, monotone inclusion reduces to a stationarity condition, which for unconstrained problems boils down to finding a point with small gradient norm.

Of particular interest to machine learning are stochastic versions of these problems, in which the operator FF is not readily available, but can only be accessed through a stochastic oracle F^\widehat{F}. Such are the settings mentioned above, where the definitions of equilibria involve expectations over continuous high-dimensional spaces. The corresponding problem, known as the stochastic monotone inclusion, has not been thoroughly studied, particularly in the context of its stochastic oracle complexity. Understanding stochastic oracle complexity of monotone inclusion in all standard settings with Lipschitz operators, from the algorithmic aspect, is the main motivation of this work.

1.1 Contributions

We study three main classes of stochastic monotone inclusion problems with Lipschitz operators, defined by the assumptions made about the operator itself: (i) cocoercive class, which is the most restricted class, but nevertheless fundamental for understanding monotone inclusion, as it relates to the problem of finding a fixed point of a nonexpansive (1-Lipschitz) operator; (ii) Lipschitz monotone class, which is perhaps the most basic class arising in the study of smooth convex-concave min-max optimization problems; and (iii) Lipschitz monotone class with an additional sharpness property of the operator. Sharpness is a widely studied property of optimization problems, often referred to as the “local error bound” condition, which is weaker than strong convexity and roughly corresponds to the problem landscape being curved outside of the solution set (see Pang (1997) for a survey of classical results).

From an algorithmic standpoint, we consider variants of classical Halpern iteration (Halpern, 1967), which was originally introduced for solving fixed point equations with nonexpansive operators. Variants of this iteration have recently been shown to lead to (near-)optimal first-order oracle complexity for all aforementioned standard problem classes in deterministic settings (Diakonikolas, 2020; Diakonikolas and Wang, 2022; Yoon and Ryu, 2021). However, to the best of our knowledge, stochastic variants of these methods have received very limited attention prior to our work. The only results we are aware of are for a two-step extragradient-like variant of Halpern iteration in negative comonotone Lipschitz settings (Lee and Kim, 2021) and which show that when variance of operator estimates is bounded by order-ϵ2k\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k} in iteration k,k, the method attains operator norm ϵ\epsilon after 𝒪⁡(1ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) iterations. However, Lee and Kim (2021) does not discuss how such variance control would be obtained. Simple mini-batching, as we show, only leads to 𝒪⁡(1ϵ4)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}}) stochastic oracle complexity.

We show that existing variants of the Halpern iteration (Diakonikolas, 2020; Tran-Dinh and Luo, 2021) can be effectively combined with recursive variance reduction (Li et al., 2021) to obtain 𝒪⁡(1ϵ3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{3}}) stochastic oracle complexity in the cocoercive and Lipschitz monotone setups. We then show that the complexity can be further reduced to 𝒪⁡(1ϵ2​log⁡(1ϵ))\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\log(\frac{1}{\epsilon})\big) under an additional sharpness assumption about the operator. The last bound is unimprovable in terms of the dependence on ϵ,\epsilon, due to existing lower bounds, as we argue for completeness in Section 7.

To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to use variance reduction to reduce stochastic oracle complexity of monotone inclusion (small gradient norm in min-max optimization settings), and the attained bounds are the best achieved to date for direct methods.

1.2 Techniques

Inspired by the potential function originally used by Diakonikolas (2020) and later used either in the same or slightly modified form by Diakonikolas and Wang (2022); Yoon and Ryu (2021); Tran-Dinh and Luo (2021); Lee and Kim (2021), we adapt this potential function-based argument to account for stochastic error terms arising due to the stochastic oracle access to the operator. We first show that in the cocoercive minibatch setting, this argument only leads to 𝒪⁡(1ϵ4)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}}) stochastic oracle complexity, and it is unclear how to improve it directly, as the analysis appears tight. We then combine the cocoercive variant of Halpern iteration (Diakonikolas, 2020) with the PAGE estimator (Li et al., 2021) to reduce the stochastic oracle complexity to 𝒪⁡(1ϵ3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{3}}). The same variance reduced estimator is also used in conjunction with the two-step extrapolated variant of Halpern iteration introduced by Tran-Dinh and Luo (2021), as a direct application of Halpern iteration is not known to converge on the class of Lipschitz monotone operators.

While the basic ideas in our arguments are simple, their realization requires addressing major technical obstacles. First, the variance reduced estimator that we use (Li et al., 2021) was originally devised for smooth nonconvex optimization problems, where it was coupled with a stochastic variant of gradient descent. This is significant, because the proof relies on a descent lemma, which allows cancelling the error arising from the variance of the estimator by the “descent” part. Such an argument is not possible in our setting, as there is no objective function to descend on. Instead, our analysis relies on an intricate inductive argument that ensures that the expected norm of the operator is bounded in each iteration, assuming a suitable bound on the variance of the estimator. To obtain our desired result for the variance, we propose a data-dependent batch allocation in PAGE estimator (Li et al., 2021) (see Corollary 2.2), which scales proportionally to the squared distance between successive iterates, similar to Arjevani et al. (2020). We inductively argue that the squared distance between successive iterates arising in the batch size of the estimator reduces at rate 1k2\frac{1}{k^{2}} in expectation. This allows us to further certify that the estimators do not only remain accurate, but their variance decreases as 𝒪⁡(ϵ2/k){\cal O}(\epsilon^{2}/k), where kk is the iteration count.

In the context of the potential function argument, unlike in the deterministic settings, we do not establish that the potential function is non-increasing, even in expectation. The stochastic error terms that arise due to the stochastic nature of the operator evaluations are controlled by taking slightly smaller step sizes than in the vanilla methods from Diakonikolas (2020); Tran-Dinh and Luo (2021), which allows us to “leak” negative quadratic terms that are further used in controlling the stochastic error. The argument for controlling the value of the potential function is itself coupled with the inductive argument for ensuring that the expected operator norm remains bounded.

Finally, while applying a restarting strategy is standard under sharpness conditions (Roulet and d’Aspremont, 2020), obtaining the claimed stochastic oracle complexity result of 𝒪⁡(1ϵ2​log⁡(1ϵ))\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\log(\frac{1}{\epsilon})\big) requires a rather technical argument to bound the total number of stochastic queries to the operator.

1.3 Related work

Monotone inclusion and variational inequalities.

Variational inequality problems were originally devised to deal with approximating equilibria. Their systematic study was initiated by Stampacchia (1964). The relationship between variational inequalities and min-max optimization was observed soon after Rockafellar (1970), while one of the earliest papers to study solving monotone inclusion as a generalization of variational inequalities, convex and min-max optimization, and complementarity problems is Rockafellar (1976). For a historical overview of this area and an extensive review of classical results, see Facchinei and Pang (2003).

In the case of monotone operators, standard variants of variational inequality problems (see Section 2) and monotone inclusion are equivalent—their solution sets coincide. This is a consequence of the celebrated Minty Theorem (Minty, 1962). However, there is a major difference between these problems when it comes to solving them to a finite accuracy. In particular, on unbounded domains, approximating variational inequalities is meaningless, whereas monotone inclusion remains well-defined. This is most readily seen from the observation that mapping from min-max optimization, variational inequalities correspond to primal-dual gap guarantees, while monotone inclusion corresponds to a guarantee in gradient norm. For a simple bilinear function f⁡(x,y)=x​yf(x,y)=xy which has the unique min-max solution at (x,y)=(0,0)(x,y)=(0,0), the primal-dual gap is infinite for any point other than (0,0),(0,0), while the gradient remains finite and is a good proxy for measuring quality of a solution. Further, even on bounded domains or using restricted gap functions on unbounded domains as in e.g., Nesterov (2007), optimal oracle complexity guarantees for approximate monotone inclusion imply optimal complexity guarantees for approximately satisfied variational inequalities (see, e.g., Diakonikolas (2020)). The opposite does not hold in general. In particular, in deterministic settings, standard algorithms such as the celebrated extragradient (Korpelevich, 1977; Nemirovski, 2004), dual extrapolation (Nesterov, 2007), or Popov’s method (Popov, 1980) that have the optimal oracle complexity O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) for approximating variational inequalities are suboptimal for monotone inclusion and attain oracle complexity of the order O⁡(1ϵ2)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}) (Golowich et al., 2020; Diakonikolas and Wang, 2022).

Halpern iteration.

Halpern iteration is a classical fixed point iteration originally introduced by Halpern (1967), and studied extensively in terms of both its asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees  (Wittmann, 1992; Leustean, 2007; Lieder, 2021; Kohlenbach, 2011; Kohlenbach and Leuştean, 2012; Cheval et al., 2022).. The first tight nonasymptotic convergence rate guarantee of 1/t1/t was obtained in Lieder (2021); Sabach and Shtern (2017). This rate was also matched by an alternative method proposed by Kim (2019).

The usefulness of Halpern iteration for solving monotone inclusion problems was first observed by Diakonikolas (2020),11 1 Interestingly, the algorithm proposed by Kim (2019) for cocoercive inclusion coincides with the Halpern iteration for a related nonexpansive operator (see Contreras and Cominetti (2021, Proposition 4.3)). who showed that its variants can be used to obtain near-optimal oracle complexity results for all standard classes of monotone inclusion problems with Lipschitz operators also studied in this work. The near-tightness (up to poly-logarithmic factors) of the results from Diakonikolas (2020) was certified using lower bound reductions from min-max optimization lower bounds introduced by Ouyang and Xu (2019). These lower bounds were made tight for the cocoercive setup in Diakonikolas and Wang (2022).

The generalization of Halpern iteration from the cocoercive to Lipschitz monotone setup in Diakonikolas (2020) utilized approximating what is known as the resolvent operator, which led to a double-loop algorithm and an additional log⁡(1/ϵ)\log(1/\epsilon) in the resulting complexity. This log factor was shaved off in Yoon and Ryu (2021), who introduced a two-step variant of Halpern iteration, inspired by the extragradient method of Korpelevich (1977). The results of Diakonikolas (2020); Yoon and Ryu (2021) were further extended to other classes of Lipschitz operators by Tran-Dinh and Luo (2021); Lee and Kim (2021). Except for Lee and Kim (2021) which considered controlled variance as discussed above, all of the existing results only targeted deterministic settings.

Stochastic settings and variance reduction.

Vanilla stochastic gradient methods have constant variance of stochastic gradients, which creates a bottleneck in the convergence rate. To improve the convergence rate, in the past decade, powerful variance reduction techniques have been proposed.

For strongly convex finite-sum problems, SAG (Schmidt et al., 2017), which used a biased stochastic estimator of the full gradient, was the first stochastic gradient method with a linear convergence rate. Johnson and Zhang (2013) and Defazio et al. (2014) improved Schmidt et al. (2017) by proposing unbiased estimators of SVRG-type and SAGA-type, respectively. Such unbiased estimators were further combined with Nesterov acceleration (Allen-Zhu, 2017; Song et al., 2020), or applied to nonconvex finite-sum/infinite-sum problems (Reddi et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2017). For nonconvex stochastic (infinite-sum) problems, SARAH (Nguyen et al., 2017) and SPIDER (Fang et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2018a; Zhou et al., 2018b) estimators were proposed to attain the optimal oracle complexity of 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ3)\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^{3}) for finding an ϵ\epsilon-approximate stationary point. Both estimators are referred to as “recursive” variance reduction estimators, as they are biased when taking expectation w.r.t. current randomness but unbiased w.r.t. all the randomness in history. PAGE (Li et al., 2021) and STORM (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019) significantly simplified SARAH and SPIDER in terms of reducing the number of loops and avoiding large minibatches, respectively. Arjevani et al. (2020) further extended this line of work by incorporating second-order information and dynamic batch sizes.

In the setting of min-max optimization and variational inequalities/monotone inclusion, variance reduction has primarily been used for approximating variational inequalities, corresponding to the primal-dual gap in min-max optimization; see, for example Palaniappan and Bach (2016); Alacaoglu and Malitsky (2022); Iusem et al. (2017); Chavdarova et al. (2019); Carmon et al. (2019); Loizou et al. (2021). Under strong monotonicity (or sharpness in the case of Loizou et al. (2021)), such results generalize to monotone inclusion; however, to the best of our knowledge, there have been no results that address monotone inclusion under the weaker assumptions considered in this work. In the context of monotone inclusion with Lipschitz operators, the tightest complexity result that we are aware of is 𝒪⁡(1ϵ4),\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}}), due to Diakonikolas et al. (2021), and it applies to a more general class of structured non-monotone Lipschitz operators, for the best iterate. The same oracle complexity can be deduced for the last iterate of a two-step variant of Halpern from Lee and Kim (2021, Theorem 6.1), using mini-batching. All the results in our work are also for the last iterate.

2 Preliminaries

We consider a real dd-dimensional normed space (ℝd,‖⋅‖)(\mathbb{R}^{d},\left\|\cdot\right\|), where ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\| is induced by an inner product associated with the space, i.e., ‖⋅‖=⟨⋅,⋅⟩\left\|\cdot\right\|=\sqrt{\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle}. Let 𝒰⊆ℝd\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be closed and convex; in the unconstrained case, 𝒰≡ℝd\mathcal{U}\equiv\mathbb{R}^{d}. When 𝒰\mathcal{U} is bounded, D=max𝐮,𝐯∈𝒰⁡‖𝐮−𝐯‖D=\max_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{U}}\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\| denotes its diameter.

Classes of monotone operators.

We say that an operator F:ℝd→ℝdF:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} is

  1. 1.

    monotone, if ∀𝐮,𝐯∈ℝd,\forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ⟨F⁡(𝐮)−F⁡(𝐯),𝐮−𝐯⟩≥0.\left\langle F(\mathbf{u})-F(\mathbf{v}),\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\rangle\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    LL-Lipschitz continuous for some L>0L>0, if ∀𝐮,𝐯∈ℝd,\forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ‖F⁡(𝐮)−F⁡(𝐯)‖≤L⁡‖𝐮−𝐯‖.\|F(\mathbf{u})-F(\mathbf{v})\|\leq L\left\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\|.

  3. 3.

    γ\gamma-cocoercive for some γ>0\gamma>0, if ∀𝐮,𝐯∈ℝd\forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ⟨F⁡(𝐮)−F⁡(𝐯),𝐮−𝐯⟩≥γ​‖F⁡(𝐮)−F⁡(𝐯)‖2.\left\langle F(\mathbf{u})-F(\mathbf{v}),\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\rangle\geq\gamma\left\|F(\mathbf{u})-F(\mathbf{v})\right\|^{2}.

  4. 4.

    μ\mu-strongly monotone for some μ>0\mu>0, if ∀𝐮,𝐯∈ℝd\forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ⟨F⁡(𝐮)−F⁡(𝐯),𝐮−𝐯⟩≥μ​‖𝐮−𝐯‖2.\left\langle F(\mathbf{u})-F(\mathbf{v}),\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\rangle\geq\mu\left\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\|^{2}.

Note that we can easily specialize these definitions to the set 𝒰\mathcal{U} by restricting 𝐮,𝐯\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} to be from 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

Throughout the paper, the minimum assumption that we make about an operator FF is that it is monotone and Lipschitz. Observe that any γ\gamma-cocoercive operator is monotone and 1γ\frac{1}{\gamma}-Lipschitz. The converse to this statement does not hold in general.

Monotone inclusion and variational inequalities.

Monotone inclusion asks for 𝐮∗\mathbf{u}^{*} such that

𝟎∈F⁡(𝐮∗)+∂I𝒰​(𝐮∗),\mathbf{0}\in F(\mathbf{u}^{*})+\partial I_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{u}^{*}), (MI)

where I𝒰I_{\mathcal{U}} is the indicator function of the set 𝒰\mathcal{U} and ∂I𝒰​(⋅)\partial I_{\mathcal{U}}(\cdot) denotes the subdifferential of I𝒰I_{\mathcal{U}}.

If FF is continuous and monotone, the solution set to (MI) is the same as the solution set of the Stampacchia Variational Inequality (SVI) problem, which asks for 𝐮∗∈𝒰\mathbf{u}^{*}\in\mathcal{U} such that

(∀𝐮∈𝒰):⟨F⁡(𝐮∗),𝐮−𝐮∗⟩≥0.(\forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U}):\quad\left\langle F\left(\mathbf{u}^{*}\right),\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\rangle\geq 0. (SVI)

Further, when FF is monotone, the solution set of (SVI) is equivalent to the solution set of the Minty Variational Inequality (MVI) problem consisting in finding 𝐮∗\mathbf{u}^{*} such that

(∀𝐮∈𝒰):⟨F⁡(𝐮),𝐮∗−𝐮⟩≤0.(\forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U}):\quad\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}),\mathbf{u}^{*}-\mathbf{u}\right\rangle\leq 0. (MVI)

We assume throughout the paper that a solution to monotone inclusion (MI) exists, which implies that solutions to both (SVI) and (MVI) exist as well. Existence of solutions follows from standard results and is guaranteed whenever e.g., 𝒰\mathcal{U} is compact, or, if there exists a compact set 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime} such that Id−1L​F\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{L}F maps 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime} to itself, where Id\mathrm{Id} is the identity map (Facchinei and Pang, 2003). As remarked in the introduction, in unbounded setups it is generally not possible to approximate (MVI) and (SVI), whereas approximating (MI) is quite natural: we only need to find 𝐮\mathbf{u} such that 0∈F⁡(𝐮)+∂I𝒰​(𝐮)+ℬ⁡(ϵ)\textbf{0}\in F(\mathbf{u})+\partial I_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{u})+\mathcal{B}(\epsilon), where 0 denotes the zero vector and ℬ⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{B}(\epsilon) denotes the centered ball of radius ϵ\epsilon.

Stochastic access to the operator.

We consider the stochastic setting for monotone inclusion problems. More specifically, we make the following assumptions for stochastic queries to F.F. These assumptions are made throughout the paper, without being explicitly invoked.

Assumption 1 (Unbiased samples with bounded variance).

For each query point 𝐱∈𝒰\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{U}, we observe F^​(𝐱,z)\widehat{F}(\mathbf{x},z) where z∼Pzz\sim P_{z} is a random variable that satisfies the following assumptions:

𝔼z​[F^​(𝐱,z)]=F⁡(𝐱) and 𝔼z​[‖F^​(𝐱,z)−F⁡(𝐱)‖2]≤σ2.\mathbb{E}_{z}\big[\widehat{F}(\mathbf{x},z)\big]=F(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathbb{E}_{z}\big[\big\|{\widehat{F}(\mathbf{x},z)-F(\mathbf{x})}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq\sigma^{2}.
Assumption 2 (Multi-point oracle).

We can query a set of points (𝐱1,…,𝐱n)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n}) and receive

F^​(𝐱1,z),…,F^​(𝐱n,z)wherez∼Pz.\widehat{F}(\mathbf{x}_{1},z),\dots,\widehat{F}(\mathbf{x}_{n},z)\quad\text{where}\quad z\sim P_{z}.
Assumption 3 (Lipschitz in expectation).

𝔼z​[‖F^​(𝐮,z)−F^​(𝐯,z)‖2]≤L2​‖𝐮−𝐯‖2\mathbb{E}_{z}\big[\big\|{\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u},z)-\widehat{F}(\mathbf{v},z)}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\right\|^{2}, ∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝒰\forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{U}.

We note that complexity results of the paper will bound the total number of queries made to this oracle. In particular, if multiple query points and/or multiple samples zz are used in a single iteration, our complexity is given by the sum of all those queries throughout all iterations of the method. Also, Assumption 3 is primary with parameter LL, by which FF is also LL-Lipschitz using Jensen’s inequality.

PAGE variance-reduced estimator.

We now summarize a variant of the PAGE estimator, originally developed for smooth nonconvex optimization by Li et al. (2021), adapted to our setting. In particular, given queries to F^\widehat{F}, we define the variance reduced estimator F~​(𝐮k)\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k}) for k≥1k\geq 1 by

F~​(𝐮k)={1S1(k)​∑i=1S1(k)F^​(𝐮k,zi(k))w. p. ​pk,F~​(𝐮k−1)+1S2(k)​∑i=1S2(k)(F^​(𝐮k,zi(k))−F^​(𝐮k−1,zi(k)))w. p. ​1−pk,\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{S_{1}^{(k)}}\sum_{i=1}^{S_{1}^{(k)}}\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k},z^{(k)}_{i})&\text{w.~p. }p_{k},\\ \widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})+\frac{1}{S_{2}^{(k)}}\sum_{i=1}^{S_{2}^{(k)}}\left(\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k},z^{(k)}_{i})-\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1},z^{(k)}_{i})\right)&\text{w.~p. }1-p_{k},\end{cases} (2.1)

where p0=1p_{0}=1, zi(k)​∼i.i.d.​Pzz^{(k)}_{i}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}P_{z}, and S1(k)S_{1}^{(k)} and S2(k)S_{2}^{(k)} are the sample sizes at iteration kk. Observe that Assumption 2 guarantees that we can query F^\widehat{F} at 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} and 𝐮k−1\mathbf{u}_{k-1} using the same random seed. Our analysis will make use of conditional expectations, and to that end, we define natural filtration ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} by ℱk:=σ⁡({F~​(𝐮j)}j≤k)\mathcal{F}_{k}:=\sigma(\{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{j})\}_{j\leq k}); namely ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} contains all the randomness that arises in the definitions of F~​(𝐮j)\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{j}) for j≤k.j\leq k. Following a similar argument as in Li et al. (2021), we recursively bound the variance of the estimator F~\widetilde{F}, as summarized in the following lemma. The proof is provided in Appendix A.

Lemma 2.1.

Let FF be a monotone operator accessed via stochastic queries F^\widehat{F}, under Assumptions 1–3. Then, the variance of F~\widetilde{F} defined by Eq. (2.1) satisfies the following recursive bound: for all k≥1,k\geq 1,

𝔼⁡[‖F~​(𝐮k)−F⁡(𝐮k)‖2]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})-F(\mathbf{u}_{k})}\|^{2}]\leq pk​σ2S1(k)+(1−pk)​(𝔼⁡[‖F~​(𝐮k−1)−F⁡(𝐮k−1)‖2]+𝔼⁡[L2​‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2S2(k)]).\displaystyle\frac{p_{k}\sigma^{2}}{S_{1}^{(k)}}+(1-p_{k})\Big(\mathbb{E}[\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})-F(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})}\|^{2}]+\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{L^{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\|^{2}}{S_{2}^{(k)}}\Big]\Big).

With the choices of pk,S1(k),S2(k)p_{k},S_{1}^{(k)},S_{2}^{(k)} specified in the following corollary and using induction with the inequality from Lemma 2.1, we obtain the following bound on the variance.

Corollary 2.2.

Given a target error ϵ>0\epsilon>0, if for all k≥1k\geq 1, pk=2k+1,S1(k)≥⌈8​σ2pk​ϵ2⌉,S2(k)≥⌈8​L2​‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2pk2​ϵ2⌉p_{k}=\frac{2}{k+1},S_{1}^{(k)}\geq\big\lceil\frac{8\sigma^{2}}{p_{k}\epsilon^{2}}\big\rceil,S_{2}^{(k)}\geq\big\lceil\frac{8L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}}{p_{k}^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\big\rceil, then 𝔼⁡[‖F~​(𝐮k)−F⁡(𝐮k)‖2]≤ϵ2k.\mathbb{E}\big[\big\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})-F(\mathbf{u}_{k})}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k}.

3 Stochastic Halpern Iteration for Cocoercive Operators

In this section, we consider the setting of 1L\frac{1}{L}-cocoercive operators F.F. While cocoercivity is a strong assumption that implies that an operator is both Lipschitz and monotone (as discussed in Section 2), it is nevertheless the most basic setup for studying the Halpern iteration. In particular, while Halpern iteration can be applied directly to the nonexpansive counterpart of a cocoercive operator FF (i.e., to the linear transformation Id−2L​F\mathrm{Id}-\frac{2}{L}F, where 1L\frac{1}{L} is an upper bound on the cocoercivity parameter of FF), convergence does not seem possible to establish for the more general class of Lipschitz monotone operators. We begin this section by providing a generic proof of stochastic oracle complexity, which we then use to briefly illustrate how to obtain 𝒪⁡(1ϵ4){\cal O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}}) oracle complexity with a simple minibatch stochastic estimator of FF. We then show how to improve this bound to 𝒪⁡(1ϵ3){\cal O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{3}}) by applying the proposed variant of the PAGE estimator from Eq. (2.1) to Halpern iteration.

The stochastic variant of Halpern iteration that we consider is defined by

𝐮k+1=λk+1​𝐮0+(1−λk+1)​(𝐮k−2Lk+1​F~​(𝐮k)),\mathbf{u}_{k+1}=\lambda_{k+1}\mathbf{u}_{0}+(1-\lambda_{k+1})\Big(\mathbf{u}_{k}-\frac{2}{L_{k+1}}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\Big), (3.1)

where F~\widetilde{F} is a stochastic (possibly biased) estimator of FF, λk+1=Θ⁡(1k)\lambda_{k+1}=\Theta(\frac{1}{k}) is the step size, and Lk+1≥LL_{k+1}\geq L is a parameter of the algorithm. Compared to the classical iteration 𝐮k+1=λk+1​𝐮0+(1−λk+1)​T​(𝐮k)\mathbf{u}_{k+1}=\lambda_{k+1}\mathbf{u}_{0}+(1-\lambda_{k+1})T(\mathbf{u}_{k}), where T:ℝd→ℝdT:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is a nonexpansive (1-Lipschitz) map (Halpern, 1967), TT is replaced by the mapping Id−2Lk+1​F~\mathrm{Id}-\frac{2}{L_{k+1}}\widetilde{F}, which is stochastic and may not be nonexpansive (as the stochastic estimate F~\widetilde{F} of FF is not guaranteed to be cocoercive even when FF is). Compared to the iteration variant considered by Diakonikolas (2020), the access to the monotone operator is stochastic and we also take slightly larger (by a factor of 2) values of Lk+1L_{k+1} to bound the stochastic error terms.

Our argument for bounding the total number of stochastic queries to FF is based on the use of the following potential function 𝒞k=AkLk​∥F⁡(𝐮k)∥2+Bk​⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮k−𝐮0⟩\mathcal{C}_{k}=\frac{A_{k}}{L_{k}}\lVert F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\rVert^{2}+B_{k}\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle, where {Ak}k≥1\{A_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} and {Bk}k≥1\{B_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} are positive and non-decreasing sequences of real numbers, while the step size λk\lambda_{k} is defined by λk:=BkAk+Bk\lambda_{k}:=\frac{B_{k}}{A_{k}+B_{k}}. Such potential function was previously used for the deterministic case of Halpern iteration in Diakonikolas (2020); Diakonikolas and Wang (2022). Observe that even though we make oracle queries to F^\widehat{F}, the potential function 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} and the final bound we obtain are in terms of the true operator value F.F.

Compared to the analysis of Halpern iteration in the deterministic case (Diakonikolas, 2020; Diakonikolas and Wang, 2022), our analysis for the stochastic case needs to account for the error terms caused by accessing FF via stochastic queries and is based on an intricate inductive argument. A generic bound on iteration complexity, under mild assumptions about the estimator F~,\widetilde{F}, is summarized in Theorem 3.1. The proof is in Appendix B.

Theorem 3.1.

Given an arbitrary 𝐮0∈ℝd,\mathbf{u}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, suppose that iterates 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} evolve according to Halpern iteration from Eq. (3.1) for k≥1,k\geq 1, where Lk=2​LL_{k}=2L and λk=1k+1.\lambda_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}. Assume further that the stochastic estimate F~​(𝐮)\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}) is unbiased for 𝐮=𝐮0\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_{0} and 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮0)−F~​(𝐮0)‖2]≤ϵ28\mathbb{E}[\|F(\mathbf{u}_{0})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\|^{2}]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{8}. Given ϵ>0,\epsilon>0, if for all k≥1,k\geq 1, we have that 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖2]≤ϵ2k\mathbb{E}\big[\big\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k}, then for all k≥1,k\geq 1,

𝔼[‖F(𝐮k))‖]≤Λ0k+Λ1ϵ,\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k}))\right\|]\leq\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{k}+\Lambda_{1}\epsilon, (3.2)

where Λ0=76​L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖\Lambda_{0}=76L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\| and Λ1=4​23\Lambda_{1}=4\sqrt{\frac{2}{{3}}}. As a result, stochastic Halpern iteration from Eq. (3.1) returns a point 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} such that 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖]≤4​ϵ\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|]\leq 4\epsilon after at most N=⌈2​Λ0ϵ⌉=𝒪⁡(L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ)N=\lceil\frac{2\Lambda_{0}}{\epsilon}\rceil=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{L\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\|}{\epsilon}\big) iterations.

We remark that the previous result states an iteration complexity bound under a rather high accuracy assumption for the operator estimators at each iteration. In order to attain these accuracy requirements, we could either use a minibatch at every iteration, or use variance reduction. In what follows we explore both approaches. We further remark that we made no effort to optimize the constants in the bound above, and thus the constants are likely improvable.

Finally, observe that due to the required low error for the estimates 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖2]≤ϵ2k,\mathbb{E}[\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|^{2}]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k}, we can certify by Chebyshev bound that ℙ[∥F(𝐮k)−F~(𝐮k)∥≥ϵ]≤1k.\mathbb{P}[\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|\geq\epsilon]\leq\frac{1}{k}. In particular, after O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) iterations, if we have ‖F~​(𝐮k)‖≤ϵ\|\tilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|\leq\epsilon (which holds in expectation), then ‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\| is also O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon) with probability at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon. This is particularly important for practical implementations, where a stopping criterion can be based on the value of ‖F~​(𝐮k)‖\|\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|, which, unlike ‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|, can be efficiently evaluated.

3.1 Stochastic Oracle Complexity With a Simple Mini-batch Estimate

A direct consequence of Theorem 3.1 is that a simple estimator F~​(𝐮k)=1Sk​∑i=1SkF^​(𝐮k,zi(k))\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})=\frac{1}{S_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{S_{k}}\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k},z_{i}^{(k)}) leads to the overall 𝒪⁡(1ϵ4)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}}) oracle complexity, as stated in the following corollary of Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 3.2.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.1, if F~​(𝐮k)=1Sk​∑i=1SkF^​(𝐮k,zi(k))\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})=\frac{1}{S_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{S_{k}}\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k},z_{i}^{(k)}), where F^​(𝐮k,zi(k))\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k},z_{i}^{(k)}) satisfies Assumption 1 and zi(k)​∼i.i.d.​Pzz^{(k)}_{i}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}P_{z}, then setting Sk=σ2​(k+1)ϵ2S_{k}=\frac{\sigma^{2}(k+1)}{\epsilon^{2}} for all k≥0k\geq 0 guarantees that 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖]≤4​ϵ\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|]\leq 4\epsilon after at most 𝒪⁡(σ2​L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2ϵ4)\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}L^{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\|^{2}}{\epsilon^{4}}\big) queries to F^\widehat{F}.

Proof.

The averaged operator from the theorem statement is unbiased, by Assumption 1. Further, as by Assumption 1, ‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F^​(𝐮k,zi(k))‖2≤σ2,\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widehat{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k},z_{i}^{(k)})\|^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}, it immediately follows that ‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖2≤σ2Sk=ϵ2k+1\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|^{2}\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{S_{k}}=\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k+1}. Applying Theorem 3.1, the total number of iterations NN of Halpern iteration until 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮N)‖]≤4​ϵ\mathbb{E}[\|F(\mathbf{u}_{N})\|]\leq 4\epsilon is N=𝒪⁡(L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ).N=\mathcal{O}(\frac{L\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\|}{\epsilon}). To complete the proof, it remains to bound the total number of oracle queries F^\widehat{F} to F,F, which is simply ∑k=0NSk=𝒪⁡(N2​σ2ϵ2)=𝒪⁡(σ2​L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2ϵ4).\sum_{k=0}^{N}S_{k}=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{N^{2}\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big)=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}L^{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\|^{2}}{\epsilon^{4}}\big). ∎

3.2 Improved Oracle Complexity via Variance Reduction

We now consider using the recursive variance reduction method from Eq. (2.1) to obtain the variance bound required in Theorem 3.1. The algorithm with all its corresponding parameter settings is summarized in Algorithm 1. Of course, in practice, ‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\| is not known, and instead of running the algorithm for a fixed number of iterations N,N, one could run it, for example, until reaching a point with ‖F~​(𝐮k)‖≤ϵ.\|\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|\leq\epsilon. Notice that convergence is guaranteed by Theorem 3.1; however it does not directly address the problem of the oracle complexity (as batch sizes depend on successive iterate distances). To resolve this issue, we first provide a bound on ‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|.

Lemma 3.3.

Given an arbitrary initial point 𝐮0∈ℝd,\mathbf{u}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, let {𝐮k}k≥1\{\mathbf{u}_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} be the sequence of points produced by Algorithm 1. Assume further that λk=1k+1\lambda_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}, Lk=2​LL_{k}=2L for all k≥0k\geq 0. Then,

‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2≤{14​L2​‖F~​(𝐮0)‖2if ​k=1,2​k2L2​(k+1)2​‖F~​(𝐮k−1)‖2+∑i=0k−22​(i+1)2k​(k+1)2​L2​‖F~​(𝐮i)‖2if ​k≥2.\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\leq\begin{cases}\frac{1}{4L^{2}}\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})}\|^{2}&\text{if }k=1,\\ \frac{2k^{2}}{L^{2}(k+1)^{2}}\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})}\|^{2}+\sum_{i=0}^{k-2}\frac{2(i+1)^{2}}{k(k+1)^{2}L^{2}}\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\|^{2}&\text{if }k\geq 2.\end{cases} (3.3)

Moreover, if for 1≤i≤k−11\leq i\leq k-1, all of the following conditions hold (same as in Theorem 3.1): (i) 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮i)‖]≤Λ0i+Λ1​ϵ,\mathbb{E}[\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\|]\leq\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{i}+\Lambda_{1}\epsilon, where Λ0=76​L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖\Lambda_{0}=76L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\| and Λ1=4​23\Lambda_{1}=4\sqrt{\frac{2}{{3}}}, (ii) 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮i)−F~​(𝐮i)‖2]≤ϵ2i\mathbb{E}\big[\big\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{i})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{i}, and (iii) ϵ≤Λ0k\epsilon\leq\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{k}, then 𝔼⁡[‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2]=𝒪⁡(‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2k2).\mathbb{E}[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}]=\mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{k^{2}}\Big).

Proof.

For k=1k=1, 𝐮1=12​𝐮0+12​(𝐮0−1L​F~​(𝐮0))\mathbf{u}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\big(\mathbf{u}_{0}-\frac{1}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\big), which leads to ‖𝐮1−𝐮0‖2=‖−12​L​F~​(𝐮0)‖2=14​L2​‖F~​(𝐮0)‖2\|{\mathbf{u}_{1}-\mathbf{u}_{0}}\|^{2}=\big\|{-\frac{1}{2L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})}\big\|^{2}=\frac{1}{4L^{2}}\big\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})}\big\|^{2}. For k≥2k\geq 2, recursively applying Eq. (3.1), we have 𝐮k−𝐮k−1=λk​(𝐮0−𝐮k−1)−1−λkL​F~​(𝐮k−1)=λk​(1−λk−1)​(𝐮0−𝐮k−2)+λk​(1−λk−1)L​F~​(𝐮k−2)−1−λkL​F~​(𝐮k−1)\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}=\lambda_{k}(\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1})-\frac{1-\lambda_{k}}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})=\lambda_{k}(1-\lambda_{k-1})(\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}_{k-2})+\frac{\lambda_{k}(1-\lambda_{k-1})}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-2})-\frac{1-\lambda_{k}}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1}), leading to

𝐮k−𝐮k−1=−1−λkL​F~​(𝐮k−1)+∑i=0k−2λkL​(∏j=i+1k−1(1−λj))​F~​(𝐮i).\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}=-\frac{1-\lambda_{k}}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})+\sum_{i=0}^{k-2}\frac{\lambda_{k}}{L}\Big(\prod_{j=i+1}^{k-1}(1-\lambda_{j})\Big)\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{i}).

Recalling that λk=1k+1\lambda_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}, we have ‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2=‖−kL⁡(k+1)​F~​(𝐮k−1)+∑i=0k−2i+1k⁡(k+1)​L​F~​(𝐮i)‖2\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}=\left\|-\frac{k}{L(k+1)}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})+\sum_{i=0}^{k-2}\frac{i+1}{k(k+1)L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{i})\right\|^{2}, which gives us Inequality (3.3) by applying a generalized variant of Young’s inequality ‖∑i=1KXi‖2≤∑i=1KK​‖Xi‖2\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{K}X_{i}\right\|^{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{K}K\left\|X_{i}\right\|^{2} twice (first to the sum of −kL⁡(k+1)​F~​(𝐮k−1)-\frac{k}{L(k+1)}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1}) and the summation term, then to the summation term, while noticing that k−1k≤1\frac{k-1}{k}\leq 1).

For the second claim, by the lemma assumptions and the analysis in the proof for Theorem 3.1, we have 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮i)‖2]=𝒪⁡(L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2i2)\mathbb{E}[\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\|^{2}]=\mathcal{O}(\frac{L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{i^{2}}) for i≤k−1≤𝒪⁡(1ϵ)i\leq k-1\leq\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\big), thus 𝔼⁡[‖F~​(𝐮i)‖2]≤2​𝔼​[‖F⁡(𝐮i)‖]2+2​𝔼​[‖F⁡(𝐮i)−F~​(𝐮i)‖2]=𝒪⁡(L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2i2)\mathbb{E}[\|{\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\|^{2}]\leq 2\mathbb{E}[\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\|]^{2}+2\mathbb{E}[\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{i})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{i})}\|^{2}]=\mathcal{O}(\frac{L^{2}\|{\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}}\|^{2}}{i^{2}}). Plugging this bound into Inequality (3.3), we get 𝔼⁡[‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2]=𝒪⁡(‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2k2)\mathbb{E}[\|{\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}}\|^{2}]=\mathcal{O}(\frac{\|{\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}}\|^{2}}{k^{2}}). ∎

Using Lemma 3.3 and making the appropriate parameter settings for the estimator from Eq. (2.1), it is now possible to apply Theorem 3.1 to obtain the improved 𝒪⁡(1ϵ3){\cal O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{3}}) stochastic oracle complexity bound, as stated in the following corollary of Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 3.4.

Given arbitrary 𝐮0∈ℝd\mathbf{u}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and ϵ>0,\epsilon>0, consider 𝐮N\mathbf{u}_{N} returned by Algorithm 1. Then, 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮N)‖]≤4​ϵ\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{N})\right\|]\leq 4\epsilon with expected 𝒪⁡(σ2​L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖+L3​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖3ϵ3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sigma^{2}L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|+L^{3}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{3}}{\epsilon^{3}}) oracle queries to F^\widehat{F}.

Proof.

Let mkm_{k} be the number of stochastic queries made by the estimator from Eq. (2.1) in iteration kk. Using Corollary 2.2, we have

𝔼⁡[mk+1|ℱk−1]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[m_{k+1}|\mathcal{F}_{k-1}\big]= pk​S1(k)+2​(1−pk)​S2(k)=pk​⌈8​σ2pk​ϵ2⌉+2​(1−pk)​⌈8​L2​‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2pk2​ϵ2⌉,\displaystyle p_{k}S_{1}^{(k)}+2(1-p_{k})S_{2}^{(k)}=p_{k}\big\lceil\textstyle\frac{8\sigma^{2}}{p_{k}\epsilon^{2}}\big\rceil+2(1-p_{k})\big\lceil\textstyle\frac{8L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}}{p_{k}^{2}\epsilon^{2}}\big\rceil,

where the first equality holds because S2(k)S_{2}^{(k)} is measurable w.r.t. ℱk−1\mathcal{F}_{k-1} and the only random choice that remains is the selection of the estimator in Eq. (2.1) determined by probabilities pkp_{k} and 1−pk.1-p_{k}.

Taking expectation with respect to all randomness on both sides, rearranging the terms, and using the fact that ⌈x⌉≤x+1\lceil x\rceil\leq x+1 for any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, we obtain 𝔼⁡[mk+1]≤8​σ2ϵ2+16​(1−pk)​L2​𝔼​[‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2]pk2​ϵ2+2\mathbb{E}[m_{k+1}]\leq\frac{8\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{16(1-p_{k})L^{2}\mathbb{E}[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}]}{p_{k}^{2}\epsilon^{2}}+2. Recalling that pk=2k+1=𝒪⁡(1k)p_{k}=\frac{2}{k+1}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k}) and 𝔼⁡[‖𝐮k−𝐮k−1‖2]=𝒪⁡(‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2k2)\mathbb{E}[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}]=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{k^{2}}\big) by Lemma 3.3, it follows that 𝔼⁡[mk+1]=𝒪⁡(σ2+L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2ϵ2)\mathbb{E}[m_{k+1}]=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}+L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big). As, by Theorem 3.1, the total number of iterations to attain 4​ϵ4\epsilon norm of the operator in expectation is N=⌈2​Λ0ϵ⌉=𝒪⁡(L⁡‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ)N=\left\lceil\frac{2\Lambda_{0}}{\epsilon}\right\rceil=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|}{\epsilon}\big) and m0=S1(0)=𝒪⁡(σ2ϵ2)m_{0}=S_{1}^{(0)}=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big), the total number of queries to F^\widehat{F} is 𝔼⁡[M]=𝔼⁡[∑k=1Nmk]=𝒪⁡(σ2​L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖+L3​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖3ϵ3)\mathbb{E}[M]=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{k=1}^{N}m_{k}]=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|+L^{3}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{3}}{\epsilon^{3}}\big). ∎

We note in passing that the running time guarantee of this algorithm is of Las Vegas-type: despite its iteration number being surely bounded by ⌈2​Λ0ϵ⌉=𝒪⁡(L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ)\big\lceil\frac{2\Lambda_{0}}{\epsilon}\big\rceil=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{L\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\|}{\epsilon}\big), the batch sizes (in particular S2(k)S_{2}^{(k)}) are random, and are not universally bounded.

We further argue that Algorithm 1 can be extended to constrained settings by defining the operator mapping as in Diakonikolas (2020) and modifying the variance-reduced stochastic estimator accordingly based on the projection of F~\widetilde{F}. We show that the newly defined operator mapping is also cocoercive while the variance of the modified estimator is bounded by the variance of F~\widetilde{F}, so arguments from Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.4 extend to this case. This modified estimator need not be unbiased (as neither is F~\widetilde{F}); however, this is irrelevant to our analysis as it does not require unbiasedness. For completeness, a detailed extension to the constrained case is provided in Appendix B.2.

4 Monotone and Lipschitz Setup

Throughout this section, we assume that FF is monotone and LL-Lipschitz. While the previous section addresses the cocoercive setup using the classical version of Halpern iteration adapted to cocoercive operators, it is unclear how to directly generalize this result to the setting with monotone Lipschitz operators. In the deterministic setting, generalization to monotone Lipschitz operators can be achieved through the use of a resolvent operator (see Diakonikolas (2020)). However, such an approach incurs an additional log⁡(1/ϵ)\log(1/\epsilon) factor in the iteration complexity coming from approximating the resolvent and it is further unclear how to generalize it to stochastic settings, as the properties of the stochastic estimate F~\widetilde{F} of FF do not readily translate into the same or similar properties for the resolvent of F~.\widetilde{F}. Instead of taking the approach based on the resolvent, we consider a recently proposed two-step variant of Halpern iteration (Tran-Dinh and Luo, 2021), adapted here to the stochastic setting. The variant uses extrapolation and is defined by

{𝐯k:=λk​𝐮0+(1−λk)​𝐮k−ηk​F~​(𝐯k−1),𝐮k+1:=λk​𝐮0+(1−λk)​𝐮k−ηk​F~​(𝐯k),\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}_{k}\quad&:=\lambda_{k}\mathbf{u}_{0}+\left(1-\lambda_{k}\right)\mathbf{u}_{k}-\eta_{k}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{v}_{k-1}),\\ \mathbf{u}_{k+1}&:=\lambda_{k}\mathbf{u}_{0}+\left(1-\lambda_{k}\right)\mathbf{u}_{k}-\eta_{k}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{v}_{k}),\end{aligned}\right. (4.1)

where λk∈[0,1)\lambda_{k}\in\left[0,1\right), ηk>0\eta_{k}>0, and F~\widetilde{F} is defined by (2.1). The resulting algorithm with a complete parameter setting is provided in Algorithm 2.

To analyze the convergence of the extrapolated Halpern variant from Eq. (4.1), we use the potential function 𝒱k=Ak​‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2+Bk​⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮k−𝐮0⟩+ck​L2​‖𝐮k−𝐯k−1‖2\mathcal{V}_{k}=A_{k}\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|^{2}+B_{k}\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle+c_{k}L^{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{v}_{k-1}\|^{2}, previously used by Tran-Dinh and Luo (2021), where AkA_{k}, BkB_{k} and ckc_{k} are positive parameters to be determined later. Observe that this is essentially the same potential function as 𝒞k,\mathcal{C}_{k}, corrected by the quadratic term ck​L2​‖𝐮k−𝐯k−1‖2c_{k}L^{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{v}_{k-1}\|^{2} to account for error terms appearing in the analysis of the two-step variant from Eq. (4.1). Similarly as in the cocoercive setup, the potential function is not monotonically non-increasing, due to the error terms that arise due to the stochastic access to F.F. Bounding these error terms requires a careful technical argument, and is the main technical contribution of this section. Due to space constraints, the complete technical argument is deferred to Appendix C, while the main results are stated below.

Theorem 4.1.

Given an arbitrary initial point 𝐮0∈ℝd\mathbf{u}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and target error ϵ>0\epsilon>0, assume that the iterates 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} evolve according to Algorithm 2 for k≥1k\geq 1. Then, for all k≥2,k\geq 2,

𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2+2​L2​‖𝐮k−𝐯k−1‖2]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}+2L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{v}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq Λ0(k+1)​(k+2)+Λ1​ϵ2,\displaystyle\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{(k+1)(k+2)}+\Lambda_{1}\epsilon^{2}, (4.2)

where Λ0=4​(L2​η0​η¯+1)​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2η¯2\Lambda_{0}=\frac{4(L^{2}\eta_{0}\underline{\eta}+1)\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{\underline{\eta}^{2}} and Λ1=5​(1+M​η¯​η0)M​η¯2\Lambda_{1}=\frac{5\left(1+M\underline{\eta}\eta_{0}\right)}{M\underline{\eta}^{2}}. In particular, 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮N)‖2+2​L2​‖𝐮N−𝐯N−1‖2]≤2​Λ1​ϵ2=𝒪⁡(ϵ2)\mathbb{E}\big[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{N})\right\|^{2}+2L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{N}-\mathbf{v}_{N-1}\right\|^{2}\big]\leq 2\Lambda_{1}\epsilon^{2}=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2}) after at most N=⌈Λ0Λ1​ϵ⌉=𝒪⁡(L⁡‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ)N=\big\lceil\frac{\sqrt{\Lambda_{0}}}{\sqrt{\Lambda_{1}}\epsilon}\big\rceil=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|}{\epsilon}\big) iterations. The total number of oracle queries to F^\widehat{F} is 𝒪⁡(σ2​L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖+L3​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖3ϵ3)\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|+L^{3}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{3}}{\epsilon^{3}}\big) in expectation.

5 Faster Convergence Under a Sharpness Condition

We now show that by restarting Algorithm 2, we can achieve the 𝒪⁡(1ϵ2​log⁡1ϵ)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right) oracle complexity under a milder than strong monotonicity μ\mu-sharpness condition: for all 𝐮∈𝒰\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U}, ⟨F⁡(𝐮)−F⁡(𝐮∗),𝐮−𝐮∗⟩≥μ​‖𝐮−𝐮∗‖2\left\langle F(\mathbf{u})-F(\mathbf{u}^{*}),\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\rangle\geq\mu\left\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}. The scheme is summarized in Algorithm 3, and the proof is deferred to Appendix D.

Theorem 5.1.

Given FF that is LL-Lipschitz and μ\mu-sharp and the precision parameter ϵ\epsilon, Algorithm 3 outputs 𝐮N\mathbf{u}_{N} with 𝔼⁡[‖𝐮N−𝐮∗‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}[\left\|\mathbf{u}_{N}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}]\leq\epsilon^{2} as well as 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮N)‖2]≤L2​ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{N})\right\|^{2}\big]\leq L^{2}\epsilon^{2} after N=𝒪⁡(Lμ​log⁡‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ)N=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L}{\mu}\log\frac{\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|}{\epsilon}\right) iterations with at most 𝒪⁡(σ2​(μ+L)​log⁡(‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖/ϵ)+L3​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2μ3​ϵ2)\mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\sigma^{2}(\mu+L)\log(\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|/\epsilon)+L^{3}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{\mu^{3}\epsilon^{2}}\Big) queries to F^\widehat{F} in expectation.

6 Numerical experiments and discussion

We now illustrate the empirical performance of stochastic Halpern iteration on robust least square problems. Specifically, given data matrix 𝐀∈ℝn×d\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and noisy observation vector 𝐛∈ℝn\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} subject to bounded deterministic perturbation δ\delta with ‖δ‖≤ρ\left\|\delta\right\|\leq\rho, robust least square (RLS) minimizes the worst-case residue as min𝐱∈ℝdmaxδ:‖δ‖≤ρ‖𝐀𝐱−𝐲‖22\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\max_{\delta:\left\|\delta\right\|\leq\rho}\left\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}_{2} with 𝐲=𝐛+δ\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}+\delta (El Ghaoui and Lebret, 1997). We consider solving MI induced from RLS with Lagrangian relaxation where 𝐮=(𝐱,𝐲)T\mathbf{u}=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})^{T} and F⁡(𝐮)=(∇𝐱Lλ​(𝐱,𝐲),−∇𝐲Lλ​(𝐱,𝐲))TF(\mathbf{u})=\big(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}L_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),-\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}L_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\big)^{T} for Lλ​(𝐱,𝐲)=12​n​‖A​𝐱−𝐲‖22−λ2​n​‖𝐲−𝐛‖22L_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\frac{1}{2n}\left\|A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}_{2}-\frac{\lambda}{2n}\left\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{b}\right\|_{2}^{2}. We use a real-world superconductivity dataset (Hamidieh, 2018) from UCI Machine Learning Repository (Dua and Graff, 2017) for our experiment, which is of size 21263×8121263\times 81. To ensure the problem is concave in 𝐲,\mathbf{y}, we need that λ>1;\lambda>1; in the experiments, we set λ=1.5\lambda=1.5.

For the experiment, we compare Halpern, E-Halpern, and Restarted E-Halpern algorithms with gradient descent-ascent (GDA), extragradient (EG) (Korpelevich, 1977), and Popov’s method (Popov, 1980) in stochastic settings. Even though our theoretical results for Restarted E-Halpern require scheduled restarts based on known problem parameters, in the implementation, to avoid complicated parameter tuning and illustrate empirical performance, we restart E-Halpern whenever the norm of stochastic estimator F~\widetilde{F} used in E-Halpern halves. All Halpern variants are implemented with PAGE estimator considered in our paper; all other algorithms are implemented using minibatches. Additionally, we compare E-Halpern with the PAGE estimator against E-Halpern with single-sample and mini-batch estimators.

We report and plot the (empirical) operator norm ‖F⁡(𝐮)‖\|F(\mathbf{u})\| against the number of stochastic operator evaluations. Note that evaluations of ‖F⁡(𝐮)‖\|F(\mathbf{u})\| are only used for plotting but not for running any of the algorithms. We use the same random initialization and tune the batch sizes and step sizes (to the values achieving fastest convergence under noise) for each method by grid search. We use constant batch sizes and constant step sizes for GDA, EG, and Popov. We also choose the batch sizes of PAGE estimator to ensure 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖2]≤𝒪⁡(1k)\mathbb{E}[\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|^{2}]\leq\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k}), which handles error accumulation (Lee and Kim, 2021) and early stagnation of stochastic Halpern iteration. We implement all the algorithms in Python and run each algorithm using one CPU core on a macOS machine with Intel 2.3GHz Dual Core i5 Processor and 8GB RAM.22 2 Code is available at https://github.com/zephyr-cai/Halpern.

We observe that (i) in Figure 1(a) both Halpern and E-Halpern exhibit faster convergence to approximate stationary points (with much smaller gradient norm after same number of gradient evaluations) than other algorithms, and restarting E-Halpern provides additional speedup, validating our theoretical insights; (ii) in Figure 1(b), E-Halpern with PAGE estimator displays faster convergence compared to other two estimators, in agreement with our theoretical analysis.

7 (Near) Tightness of Stochastic Oracle Complexity Bounds

In this section, we briefly discuss lower bound reductions which imply that our results for Lipschitz sharp setups are unimprovable in terms of the dependence on ϵ.\epsilon. To keep the discussion simple, we only focus on the ϵ\epsilon dependence here and unconstrained settings. The near-optimality of our bounds is implied by the known lower bound for the optimality gap in LL-smooth μ\mu-strongly convex stochastic optimization, which is of the order Ω⁡(σ2μ​ϵ)\Omega(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\mu\epsilon}) in the high noise σ2\sigma^{2} or low error ϵ\epsilon regimes; see, for example, the discussion in Ghadimi and Lan (2016) (the omitted part of the lower bound comes from the deterministic complexity of smooth strongly convex optimization and is less interesting in our context). The same lower bound implies a lower bound of Ω⁡(σ2ϵ2)\Omega(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}) for minimizing the gradient of a smooth strongly convex function ff. Suppose not (for the purpose of contradiction); i.e., suppose that there were an algorithm that constructs a point 𝐱\mathbf{x} with 𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(𝐱)‖2]≤ϵ¯2\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}]\leq\bar{\epsilon}^{2} in o⁡(σ2ϵ¯2)o(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\bar{\epsilon}^{2}}) oracle queries to the stochastic gradient. By μ\mu-strong convexity of f,f, this would imply that we get 𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐱)−min𝐮⁡f⁡(𝐮)]≤12​μ​𝔼​[‖∇f​(𝐱)‖2]≤ϵ¯22​μ\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x})-\min_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u})]\leq\frac{1}{2\mu}\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}]\leq\frac{\bar{\epsilon}^{2}}{2\mu} with o⁡(σ2ϵ¯2)o(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\bar{\epsilon}^{2}}) oracle queries to the stochastic gradient. Setting ϵ¯=ϵ​μ,\bar{\epsilon}=\sqrt{{\epsilon}{\mu}}, we get that this would imply oracle complexity o⁡(σ2μ​ϵ)o(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\mu\epsilon}), and we reach a contradiction on the lower bound for the optimality gap.

Hence, Ω⁡(σ2ϵ2)\Omega(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}) lower bound applies to the minimization of the gradient of smooth strongly convex functions in stochastic regimes. Observe that the gradients of smooth strongly convex functions are Lipschitz and strongly monotone (thus also sharp), so a lower bound for this problem class implies a lower bound for the class of sharp Lipschitz monotone inclusion problems. Thus, we can conclude that our result from Section 5 for sharp Lipschitz monotone inclusion problems that gives 𝒪⁡(σ2​(μ+L)​log⁡(‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖/ϵ)+L3​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2μ3​ϵ2)\mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\sigma^{2}(\mu+L)\log(\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|/\epsilon)+L^{3}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}}{\mu^{3}\epsilon^{2}}\Big) stochastic oracle complexity is near-optimal in terms of the dependence on σ\sigma and ϵ\epsilon (but likely not near-optimal in terms of the dependence on the remaining problem parameters).

8 Conclusion

We introduced stochastic variance reduced variants of Halpern iteration for addressing monotone inclusion problems. Our work addresses all standard classes of Lipschitz monotone problems and achieves improved stochastic oracle complexity guarantees, all for the last iterate. Subsequent to this work, Chen and Luo (2022) obtained near-optimal bounds for the cases considered in this work, by reducing the Lipschitz monotone case to the Lipschitz strongly monotone case, using regularization. It is an open question to obtain such near-optimal bounds with a direct method, without the use of regularization.

Appendix B Omitted proofs from Section 3

B.1 Unconstrained settings

Our argument for bounding the total number of stochastic queries to FF is based on the use of the following potential function, which was previously used for the deterministic case of Halpern iteration in (Diakonikolas, 2020; Diakonikolas and Wang, 2022),

𝒞k=AkLk​∥F⁡(𝐮k)∥2+Bk​⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮k−𝐮0⟩,\mathcal{C}_{k}=\frac{A_{k}}{L_{k}}\lVert F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\rVert^{2}+B_{k}\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle, (B.1)

where {Ak}k≥1\{A_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} and {Bk}k≥1\{B_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} are positive and non-decreasing sequences of real numbers, while the step size λk\lambda_{k} is defined by λk:=BkAk+Bk\lambda_{k}:=\frac{B_{k}}{A_{k}+B_{k}}. We start the proof by first justifying that a bound on the chosen potential function 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} leads to a bound on ‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\| in expectation. The proof is a simple extension of (Diakonikolas, 2020, Lemma 4) and is provided for completeness.

Lemma B.1.

Given k≥1,k\geq 1, let 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} be defined as in Eq. (B.1) and let 𝐮∗\mathbf{u}^{*} be a solution to the monotone inclusion problem corresponding to FF. If 𝔼⁡[𝒞k]≤𝔼⁡[ℰk]\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{k}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right] for some error term ℰk\mathcal{E}_{k}, then

𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2]≤Bk​LkAk​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖​𝔼​[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk],\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right], (B.2)

where the expectation is taken with respect to all random queries to FF.

Proof.

By the definition of 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}, we have

𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq Bk​LkAk​𝔼​[⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮0−𝐮k⟩]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk]\displaystyle\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}_{k}\right\rangle\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right]
=\displaystyle= Bk​LkAk​𝔼​[⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮0−𝐮∗+𝐮∗−𝐮k⟩]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk]\displaystyle\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}+\mathbf{u}^{*}-\mathbf{u}_{k}\right\rangle\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right]
=\displaystyle= Bk​LkAk​𝔼​[⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮0−𝐮∗⟩]+Bk​LkAk​𝔼​[⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮∗−𝐮k⟩]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk].\displaystyle\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\rangle\right]+\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}^{*}-\mathbf{u}_{k}\right\rangle\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right].

Since 𝐮∗\mathbf{u}^{*} is a solution to the monotone inclusion problem, as discussed in Section 2, it is also a weak VI (or MVI) solution, and thus

(∀k≥0)⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮∗−𝐮k⟩≤0.(\forall k\geq 0)\quad\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}^{*}-\mathbf{u}_{k}\right\rangle\leq 0.

As a result,

𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq Bk​LkAk​𝔼​[⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮0−𝐮∗⟩]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk]\displaystyle\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\rangle\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right]
≤(i)\displaystyle\overset{(i)}{\leq} Bk​LkAk​𝔼​[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk]\displaystyle\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right]
=(i​i)\displaystyle\overset{(ii)}{=} Bk​LkAk​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖​𝔼​[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖]+LkAk​𝔼​[ℰk],\displaystyle\frac{B_{k}L_{k}}{A_{k}}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|\right]+\frac{L_{k}}{A_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{E}_{k}\right],

where we use Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for (i)(i), while (i​i)(ii) holds because ‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\| involves no randomness. ∎

Using Lemma B.1, our goal now is to show that we can provide a bound on 𝔼⁡[𝒞k]\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{C}_{k}] by appropriately choosing the algorithm parameters. In the deterministic setup, it is sufficient to choose Lk=𝒪⁡(L)L_{k}=\mathcal{O}(L) and λk=𝒪⁡(1k)\lambda_{k}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k}) to ensure that {Ak​𝒞k}k≥1\{A_{k}\mathcal{C}_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} is monotonically non-increasing, which immediately leads to 𝒞k≤A1Ak​𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{k}\leq\frac{A_{1}}{A_{k}}\mathcal{C}_{1}. In the stochastic setup considered here, we follow the same motivation, but need to deal with additional error terms caused by the stochastic access to FF.

We assume throughout that LL is known, and make the following assumption on the choice of {Ak}k≥1\{A_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}, {Bk}k≥1\{B_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}, and {Lk}k≥1\{L_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}, and provide a corresponding bound on the change of 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} in Lemma B.2.

Assumption 4.

{Lk}k≥1\{L_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} is a sequence of positive reals such that Lk≥LL_{k}\geq L for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. Sequences {Ak}k≥1\{A_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} and {Bk}k≥1\{B_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} are positive and non-decreasing, satisfying the following for all k≥2k\geq 2:

Bk−1Ak=BkAk+Bk,1Lk​(1−2​BkAk+Bk)=Ak−1Ak​Lk−1.\frac{B_{k-1}}{A_{k}}=\frac{B_{k}}{A_{k}+B_{k}},\qquad\frac{1}{L_{k}}\left(1-\frac{2B_{k}}{A_{k}+B_{k}}\right)=\frac{A_{k-1}}{A_{k}L_{k-1}}.
Lemma B.2.

Let 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} be defined as in Eq. (B.1), where {Ak}k≥1\{A_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} and {Bk}k≥1\{B_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} satisfy Assumption 4. Let Lk=2​LL_{k}=2L for all k≥1k\geq 1. Then, for any k≥2k\geq 2, we have

𝒞k−𝒞k−1≤Ak2​L​‖F⁡(𝐮k−1)−F~​(𝐮k−1)‖2+Ak−Ak−12​L​⟨F⁡(𝐮k−1),F⁡(𝐮k−1)−F~​(𝐮k−1)⟩.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{k}-\mathcal{C}_{k-1}\leq\frac{A_{k}}{2L}\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})\right\|^{2}+\frac{A_{k}-A_{k-1}}{2L}\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k-1}),F(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})\right\rangle.
Proof.

By the definition of 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}, we have

𝒞k−𝒞k−1=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{k}-\mathcal{C}_{k-1}= AkLk​‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2+Bk​⟨F⁡(𝐮k),𝐮k−𝐮0⟩\displaystyle\frac{A_{k}}{L_{k}}\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}+B_{k}\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle
−Ak−1Lk−1​‖F⁡(𝐮k−1)‖2−Bk−1​⟨F⁡(𝐮k−1),𝐮k−1−𝐮0⟩.\displaystyle-\frac{A_{k-1}}{L_{k-1}}\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k-1})\right\|^{2}-B_{k-1}\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{k-1}),\mathbf{u}_{k-1}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle.

Since the operator FF is cocoercive with parameter 1L\frac{1}{L}, we have

By Lemma B.2, if we choose Ak=𝒪⁡(k2)A_{k}=\mathcal{O}(k^{2}) and Bk=𝒪⁡(k)B_{k}=\mathcal{O}(k) satisfying Assumption 4, and take sufficiently large size of samples queried to ensure that 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖2]≤ϵ2k\mathbb{E}\big[\big\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k} for k≥0k\geq 0, then we can obtain 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}(1/k) expected convergence rate in the norm of the operator by induction. Observe that we do not need an assumption that F~\widetilde{F} is an unbiased estimator of FF for any point except for the initial one; all that is needed is that the second moment of the estimation error, ‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖22\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}, is bounded.

Proof.

Observe first that the chosen sequence of numbers Ak,BkA_{k},B_{k} satisfies Assumption 4, and thus Lemma B.2 applies. Observe further that, by Jensen’s Inequality,

𝔼[‖F(𝐮k))‖]≤(𝔼[‖F(𝐮k)‖2])12.\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k}))\right\|]\leq\Big(\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}]\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

and, thus, to prove the theorem, it suffices to show that there exists Λ0\Lambda_{0} and Λ1\Lambda_{1} such that for all k≥1k\geq 1

(𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)‖2])12≤Λ0k+Λ1​ϵ.\Big(\mathbb{E}[\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}]\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{k}+\Lambda_{1}\epsilon.

𝒞1=1L​‖F⁡(𝐮1)‖2+2​⟨F⁡(𝐮1),𝐮1−𝐮0⟩=1L​(‖F⁡(𝐮1)‖2−⟨F⁡(𝐮1),F~​(𝐮0)⟩).\mathcal{C}_{1}=\frac{1}{L}\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{1})\right\|^{2}+2\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{1}),\mathbf{u}_{1}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{L}\Big(\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{1})\right\|^{2}-\left\langle F(\mathbf{u}_{1}),\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\rangle\Big). (B.3)

Further, since the operator FF is cocoercive with parameter 1L\frac{1}{L}, it is also cocoercive with parameter 12​L\frac{1}{2L}, and thus we have

Expanding and rearranging the terms, we have

≤(i)\displaystyle\overset{(i)}{\leq} 𝔼⁡[12​‖F⁡(𝐮1)‖2+2​‖F⁡(𝐮0)−F~​(𝐮0)‖2],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{2}\big\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{1})}\big\|^{2}+2\big\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{0})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})}\big\|^{2}\Big],

B.2 Constrained setting with a cocoercive operator

To extend the results to possibly constrained settings, similar to Diakonikolas (2020), we make use of the operator mapping defined by

Gη​(𝐮)=η⁡(𝐮−Π𝒰​(𝐮−1η​F​(𝐮))),\displaystyle G_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})=\eta\Big(\mathbf{u}-\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\big(\mathbf{u}-\frac{1}{\eta}F(\mathbf{u})\big)\Big), (B.7)

where 𝒰⊆ℝd\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is the closed convex constraint set and Π𝒰​(𝐮)\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{u}) is the projection operator. Operator GηG_{\eta} is a valid proxy for approximating (MI); see (Diakonikolas, 2020) for further details.

The extension of our results to constrained stochastic settings is not immediate; the reason is that the stochastic query assumptions (Assumptions 1 and 2) are made for the operator FF, not Gη.G_{\eta}. Nevertheless, as we show in this subsection, it is not hard to match the stochastic oracle complexity of the unconstrained setups by proving an additional auxiliary result that bounds the variance of an operator mapping corresponding to F~\widetilde{F} (Lemma B.4).

We begin by recalling that whenever FF is 1L\frac{1}{L}-cocoercive and η≥L\eta\geq L, the operator mapping GηG_{\eta} is 34​η\frac{3}{4\eta}-cocoercive (see, e.g., (Diakonikolas, 2020, Proposition 7) and (Beck, 2017, Lemma 10.11)).

Proposition B.3.

Let FF be 1L\frac{1}{L}-cocoercive and let GηG_{\eta} be defined as in Eq. (B.7), where η≥L\eta\geq L. Then GηG_{\eta} is 34​η\frac{3}{4\eta}-cocoercive.

To state the variant of stochastic Halpern iteration for constrained settings, we also define the operator mapping corresponding to the stochastic estimate F~\widetilde{F} by

G~η​(𝐮)=η⁡(𝐮−Π𝒰​(𝐮−1η​F~​(𝐮))).\displaystyle\widetilde{G}_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})=\eta\Big(\mathbf{u}-\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\big(\mathbf{u}-\frac{1}{\eta}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u})\big)\Big). (B.8)

In the following lemma, we bound the error between the stochastic operator mapping and true operator mapping by the variance of stochastic queries.

Lemma B.4.

Let Gη​(⋅)G_{\eta}(\cdot) and G~η​(⋅)\widetilde{G}_{\eta}(\cdot) be defined as in Eq. (B.7) and Eq. (B.8), respectively. Then, for any 𝐮∈𝒰\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U} and any η>0\eta>0, we have

‖Gη​(𝐮)−G~η​(𝐮)‖2≤‖F⁡(𝐮)−F~​(𝐮)‖2.\|{G_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})-\widetilde{G}_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})}\|^{2}\leq\|{F(\mathbf{u})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u})}\|^{2}. (B.9)
Proof.

By the definition of gradient mapping, we have

‖Gη​(𝐮)−G~η​(𝐮)‖2=η2​‖Π𝒰​(𝐮−1η​F​(𝐮))−Π𝒰​(𝐮−1η​F~​(𝐮))‖2.\displaystyle\left\|G_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})-\widetilde{G}_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})\right\|^{2}=\eta^{2}\Big\|\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\Big(\mathbf{u}-\frac{1}{\eta}F(\mathbf{u})\Big)-\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\Big(\mathbf{u}-\frac{1}{\eta}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u})\Big)\Big\|^{2}.

Since the projection operator is non-expansive, we obtain

‖Gη​(𝐮)−G~η​(𝐮)‖2≤\displaystyle\left\|G_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})-\widetilde{G}_{\eta}(\mathbf{u})\right\|^{2}\leq η2​‖(𝐮−1η​F​(𝐮))−(𝐮−1η​F~​(𝐮))‖2=‖F⁡(𝐮)−F~​(𝐮)‖2,\displaystyle\eta^{2}\Big\|\Big(\mathbf{u}-\frac{1}{\eta}F(\mathbf{u})\Big)-\Big(\mathbf{u}-\frac{1}{\eta}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u})\Big)\Big\|^{2}=\left\|F(\mathbf{u})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u})\right\|^{2},

thus completing the proof. ∎

Similar to the unconstrained setup, we define the following stochastic Halpern iteration for the constrained setup:

𝐮k+1=λk+1​𝐮0+(1−λk+1)​(𝐮k−G~Lk​(𝐮k)/Lk+1),\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{k+1}=\lambda_{k+1}\mathbf{u}_{0}+(1-\lambda_{k+1})\big(\mathbf{u}_{k}-\widetilde{G}_{L_{k}}(\mathbf{u}_{k})/L_{k+1}\big), (B.10)

where Lk≥LL_{k}\geq L, ∀k≥0\forall k\geq 0. By the cocoercivity of the operator mapping and the error bound in Lemma B.4, we can immediately obtain the results for the iteration complexity and stochastic oracle complexity as in the unconstrained case, by applying Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.4 to GLG_{L} and G~L\widetilde{G}_{L}. This is summarized in the following Theorem B.6 and Corollary B.7. To prove these, we make use of the potential function as in the unconstrained settings

𝒞k=Ak2​Lk​∥GLk​(𝐮k)∥2+Bk​⟨GLk​(𝐮k),𝐮k−𝐮0⟩,\mathcal{C}_{k}=\frac{A_{k}}{2L_{k}}\lVert G_{L_{k}}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\rVert^{2}+B_{k}\left\langle G_{L_{k}}(\mathbf{u}_{k}),\mathbf{u}_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle, (B.11)

Theorem B.6.

Given an arbitrary 𝐮0∈ℝd,\mathbf{u}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, suppose that iterates 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} evolve according to Halpern iteration for the constrained setup from Eq. (B.10) for k≥1,k\geq 1, where Lk=LL_{k}=L and λk=1k+1.\lambda_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}. Given ϵ>0,\epsilon>0, if we have that 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮0)−F~​(𝐮0)‖2]≤ϵ28\mathbb{E}[\|F(\mathbf{u}_{0})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\|^{2}]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{8} and 𝔼⁡[‖F⁡(𝐮k)−F~​(𝐮k)‖2]≤ϵ2k\mathbb{E}\big[\big\|{F(\mathbf{u}_{k})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})}\big\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k} for all k≥1k\geq 1, then for all k≥1,k\geq 1,

𝔼[‖G(𝐮k))‖]≤Λ0k+Λ1ϵ,\mathbb{E}[\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{k}))\right\|]\leq\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{k}+\Lambda_{1}\epsilon, (B.12)

where Λ0=20​L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖\Lambda_{0}=20L\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\| and Λ1=13\Lambda_{1}=\sqrt{13}. As a result, stochastic Halpern iteration from Eq. (3.1) returns a point 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} such that 𝔼⁡[‖G⁡(𝐮k)‖]≤5​ϵ\mathbb{E}[\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|]\leq 5\epsilon after at most N=⌈2​Λ0ϵ⌉=𝒪⁡(L​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖ϵ)N=\lceil\frac{2\Lambda_{0}}{\epsilon}\rceil=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{L\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\|}{\epsilon}\big) iterations.

Proof.

First note that since 𝒰\mathcal{U} is convex and closed, and 𝐮k−G~​(𝐮k)/L=Π𝒰​(𝐮k−1L​F~​(𝐮k))\mathbf{u}_{k}-\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{k})/L=\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\Big(\mathbf{u}_{k}-\frac{1}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\Big), then we have for ∀k>0\forall k>0.

𝐮k+1=\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{k+1}= λk+1​𝐮0+(1−λk+1)​(𝐮k−G~​(𝐮k)/L)\displaystyle\lambda_{k+1}\mathbf{u}_{0}+(1-\lambda_{k+1})\Big(\mathbf{u}_{k}-\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{k})/L\Big)
=\displaystyle= λk+1​𝐮0+(1−λk+1)​Π𝒰​(𝐮k−1L​F~​(𝐮k))∈𝒰.\displaystyle\lambda_{k+1}\mathbf{u}_{0}+(1-\lambda_{k+1})\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\Big(\mathbf{u}_{k}-\frac{1}{L}\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{k})\Big)\in\mathcal{U}.

Then we come to prove the convergence. By Jensen’s Inequality, we have for k≥1k\geq 1

𝔼[‖G(𝐮k))‖]≤(𝔼[‖G(𝐮k)‖2])12.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{k}))\right\|]\leq\Big(\mathbb{E}[\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{k})\right\|^{2}]\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

So it suffices to show that there exists Λ0\Lambda_{0} and Λ1\Lambda_{1} such that for all k≥1k\geq 1

We prove it by induction. First, we consider the basis case k=1k=1 in which 𝐮1=𝐮0−12​L​G~​(𝐮0)\mathbf{u}_{1}=\mathbf{u}_{0}-\frac{1}{2L}\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{0}), so we have 𝒞1=1L​‖G⁡(𝐮1)‖2+2​⟨G⁡(𝐮1),𝐮1−𝐮0⟩=1L​(‖G⁡(𝐮1)‖2−⟨G⁡(𝐮1),G~​(𝐮0)⟩)\mathcal{C}_{1}=\frac{1}{L}\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{1})\right\|^{2}+2\left\langle G(\mathbf{u}_{1}),\mathbf{u}_{1}-\mathbf{u}_{0}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{L}\Big(\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{1})\right\|^{2}-\left\langle G(\mathbf{u}_{1}),\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\rangle\Big). ≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼⁡[⟨G⁡(𝐮0),G~​(𝐮0)−G⁡(𝐮0)⟩+2​⟨G⁡(𝐮1),G⁡(𝐮0)⟩−2​⟨G⁡(𝐮1),G~​(𝐮0)⟩]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\left\langle G(\mathbf{u}_{0}),\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{0})-G(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\rangle+2\left\langle G(\mathbf{u}_{1}),G(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\rangle-2\left\langle G(\mathbf{u}_{1}),\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\rangle\Big]
≤(i)\displaystyle\overset{(i)}{\leq} 𝔼⁡[12​‖G⁡(𝐮0)‖2+12​‖G⁡(𝐮1)‖2+52​‖G⁡(𝐮0)−G~​(𝐮0)‖2],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{2}\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{1})\right\|^{2}+\frac{5}{2}\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{0})-\widetilde{G}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\|^{2}\Big],

‖G⁡(𝐮0)‖2=‖G⁡(𝐮0)−G⁡(𝐮∗)‖2​≤(i)​10​L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2,\displaystyle\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\|^{2}=\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{0})-G(\mathbf{u}^{*})\right\|^{2}\overset{(i)}{\leq}10L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2},

Proceeding similar to Lemma B.1, we have

+2​L1A1​L​𝔼​[5​L2​‖𝐮0−𝐮∗‖2+12​‖G⁡(𝐮1)‖2+52​‖F⁡(𝐮0)−F~​(𝐮0)‖2]\displaystyle+\frac{2L_{1}}{A_{1}L}\mathbb{E}\Big[5L^{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{0}-\mathbf{u}^{*}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|G(\mathbf{u}_{1})\right\|^{2}+\frac{5}{2}\left\|F(\mathbf{u}_{0})-\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{u}_{0})\right\|^{2}\Big]

Corollary B.7.

Given an arbitrary 𝐮0∈ℝd,\mathbf{u}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, suppose that iterates 𝐮k\mathbf{u}_{k} evolve according to Halpern iteration from Eq. (B.10) for k≥1,k\geq 1, where Lk=LL_{k}=L, and λk=1k+1\lambda_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}.
